subject: Running time for different parameterization methods

messages.author: 7d6ebbd01e450240
messages.subject: Running time for different parameterization methods
parts:
Hi,
We have been running some models looking at measurement invariance of a bifactor model with ordinal data. We followed the approach of Wu and Estabrook (2016), using the semtools function. We have about 10,000 participants and 67 items in the model. When we run the model with theta parameterization it takes a very long time to complete. When we run the model with delta parameterization it is somewhat faster, but still takes a couple of hours. Also, the wisdom seems to be to go with theta parameterization. Model fit seems pretty good and there do not seem to be any major problems with model estimates. 

What should I be looking for to try and speed up the model estimation? 

Thanks in advance!

Burt

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Running time for different parameterization methods
parts: 67 items in the model. When we run the model with theta parameterization it takes a very long time to complete. When we run the model with delta parameterization it is somewhat faster, but still takes a couple of hours.
With so many ordinal variables, that is no surprise.  Inverting such a large weight matrix is computationally intensive.
the wisdom seems to be to go with theta parameterization.

What wisdom?  If you are not explicitly testing hypotheses about constraints on residual variances, then the 2 parameterizations are statistically equivalent.  The Mplus documentation noted long ago that the delta is more stable, likely because residual variances can be negative (often to to sampling error, but with your very large sample, it could be a sign of misspecification).  If you have a negative residual variance using delta, then that would obviously create a problem for an optimizer looking for a solution that fixes the residual variance to 1 using theta.

Speed is less virtuous than validity of results, but you could try analyzing your data as continuous, if there are several categories (or even if not: Robitzsch, 2020).  It's a matter of choosing one set of unlikely assumptions over another.  At least when treating as continuous, you can adjust for nonnormality.  If latent responses are not normal, there is no correction for that.
